poster.title: Call to Arms
poster.bookOrigin: Chinese-language story collection by Lu Xun, originally published in 1923; the selected museum object is catalogued 1926.
poster.creator: Lu Xun
poster.alt: A large red cover surrounds a small black label with red Chinese title and author characters, a fine inset frame and short wavy divider.
poster.blurb: A compact label carries almost all the information in a large red field.

notes.title: The displayed edition
notes.body: The exact object is catalogued 1926 by NAMOC and Beijing Lu Xun Museum. The particular impression is unspecified. The collection first appeared in 1923; this image is not labelled a 1923 first-edition cover.

notes.title: Writing and image-making
notes.body: The museum caption identifies Lu Xun as both author and cover designer. The object belongs to Beijing Lu Xun Museum; early title-lettering changes are documented separately by China Publishing Museum.

notes.title: A visible design relationship
notes.body: The title is read right to left on this object. A thin red rectangle repeats the label’s outer boundary inside the black field.

studyData.intro: A small dark label concentrates the information within a broad red cover. The museum dates this object to 1926; the collection’s original 1923 publication and early lettering changes are explained separately.

regions.label: Two characters carry the title
regions.summary: Two red title characters sit near the top of the small black label.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: Two red title characters sit near the top of the small black label. On this object they are read from the right-hand character to the left.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: Reversing red out of the black field connects the writing to the much larger red surround. The same colour acts as both background and readable mark.

sections.heading: Read the title from the right
sections.body: The title is read 吶喊, Nàhǎn, from the right-hand character to the left on this object. Call to Arms is a familiar English title for the collection; it is not a letter-for-letter translation of the visible characters.
sections.translation: Nàhǎn; a cry or shout / Call to Arms

regions.question: How does red change its role when it moves inside the black rectangle?

regions.label: A smaller name below the title
regions.summary: The author characters sit beneath the wavy divider in a smaller red line.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: The author characters sit beneath the wavy divider in a smaller red line. They use the same colour contrast as the title but occupy less area.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The change of scale distinguishes author from work while keeping both in one compact label. The divider makes the distinction legible without introducing a new colour.

sections.heading: The writer also designs the cover
sections.body: The museum caption names Lu Xun as both writer and cover designer. China Publishing Museum records the collection’s 1923 first publication and explains that the initial typeset title changed in an early later edition. That history does not identify this 1926 copy as the first printing.

regions.question: Which cues separate title and author when their colours are the same?

regions.label: A concentrated dark rectangle
regions.summary: A small black rectangle occupies the upper middle of the red cover.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A small black rectangle occupies the upper middle of the red cover. Its surface contains the title, author, inset border and small decorative lines.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: Concentrating almost all detail in one small area makes the larger red field more forceful. The label can draw attention through contrast rather than sheer size.

regions.question: Why can a relatively small dark area dominate such a large red surface?

regions.label: A second frame inside the first
regions.summary: A thin red rectangular rule sits inside the dark label.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A thin red rectangular rule sits inside the dark label. It leaves a narrow black margin between itself and the label’s outer boundary.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: Repeating the rectangular enclosure gives the small label internal order. The slight inset also separates the lettering from the edge without adding much visual weight.

regions.question: What does the narrow black margin contribute to the label’s clarity?

regions.label: A wave between two names
regions.summary: A short red undulating line crosses the label between the title and author.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A short red undulating line crosses the label between the title and author. It contrasts with the straight inset frame.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The small curve introduces a different rhythm into an otherwise rectilinear structure. It can act as a pause in reading without becoming a separate illustration.

regions.question: Would a straight divider produce the same pause?

regions.label: A short line closes the label
regions.summary: A short red horizontal line sits below the author characters.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A short red horizontal line sits below the author characters. It is narrower than the surrounding frame and simpler than the wave above.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: This small mark gives the internal stack a visual ending. It helps the label feel composed as a unit rather than as unrelated text floating on black.

regions.question: How does this short final line affect the balance of the label?

regions.label: Most of the cover stays open
regions.summary: A broad expanse of muted red paper extends below the label.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A broad expanse of muted red paper extends below the label. The photographed surface contains subtle wear and tonal variation.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The large unprinted area makes the concentrated label feel deliberate. The design asks one strong relationship to do the work of many separate illustrations.

regions.question: What happens to the label’s force if this lower field is filled with more writing?

regions.label: A label above the centre
regions.summary: The label lies above the cover’s vertical midpoint.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: The label lies above the cover’s vertical midpoint. More red space remains beneath it than above it.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The raised placement changes the balance of an otherwise simple composition. It can make the lower field feel like a long pause after the title is read.

regions.question: Would a perfectly centred label feel as spacious?

regions.label: Uneven strokes within a strict frame
regions.summary: The title strokes vary in thickness and direction inside the straight rectangle.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: The title strokes vary in thickness and direction inside the straight rectangle. Small turns and tapered ends remain visible in the enlarged reproduction.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: The contrast between writing and enclosure prevents the label from becoming purely geometric. The strokes invite reading as formed marks as well as language.

regions.question: Which letter strokes most clearly resist the rigid geometry around them?

regions.label: The image preserves an actual object
regions.summary: A narrow pale edge and uneven boundary remain along the photographed cover.

sections.heading: Visible in the cover
sections.body: A narrow pale edge and uneven boundary remain along the photographed cover. The red surface does not form a perfectly flat digital rectangle.

sections.heading: A possible reading
sections.body: These physical details distinguish a museum object from a recreated graphic. They also caution against treating slight skew as an intentional typographic effect.

sections.heading: An object dated 1926
sections.body: NAMOC’s exhibition caption dates the reproduced book to 1926 and identifies Beijing Lu Xun Museum as the holding collection. The particular impression is not established here. The displayed date therefore belongs to the catalogued object, while 1923 remains the original work date.

regions.question: Which small irregularities tell you that this is a photograph of a book?

rows.meaning: Nàhǎn: a cry or shout; this collection is commonly called Call to Arms in English.

connections.title: A small label in red
connections.text: The label occupies little area while carrying almost all the cover’s information.
